Black Hills to Invest $1.8B to Power Google Data Center in Wyoming

Black Hills Corp., an energy utility in South Dakota, has signed long-term agreements to serve Google’s planned data center in Cheyenne, Wyoming, establishing a power architecture that combines up to 590 MW of grid-connected service with approximately 2.1 GW of third-party resources managed through a private microgrid. The agreements, effective September 30, run through 2048 and call for Black Hills to invest $1.8 billion between 2027 and 2029 in 564 MW of new company-owned natural gas generation. The data center is expected to begin taking power in late 2027 and ramp toward peak load in 2030. The overall resource portfolio is expected to reach approximately 2.7 GW including reserve margins. Black Hills will provide up to 590 MW of grid-connected service using its own generation and market energy, while approximately 2.1 GW of Wyoming-based third-party contracted resources will be coordinated through a privately managed microgrid under the company’s Large Power Contract Service tariff. Google Cheyenne — Power Architecture Black Hills Investment $1.8 billion during 2027–2029 Total Resource Mix ~2.7 GW , including reserve margins Grid Service Up to 590 MW New Generation 564 MW natural gas generation owned by Black Hills affiliate Third-Party Resources ~2.1 GW of Wyoming-based contracted resources Architecture Privately managed microgrid + utility grid connection Initial Service Late 2027 Peak Load Ramp Targeted for 2030 Contract Term Through 2048 The 564 MW of new gas generation will be constructed at Black Hills’ existing Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station and owned through a non-regulated affiliate. The remaining 26 MW required to provide the 590 MW grid-connected service will come from a combination of market purchases and retail utility service. The arrangement also gives Black Hills a second revenue stream beyond generation. The company will receive microgrid management fees for coordinating grid operations, reliability services and energy dispatch across the contracted third-party resources and market purchases serving the Google facility. Black Hills expects the project to contribute approximately $150 million in net income in 2030 and generate about $2.4 billion of unlevered free cash flow through 2048, net of the $1.8 billion generation investment. The company said Google has already provided $399 million in refundable advances for procurement of long-lead-time generation equipment. Black Hills expects to reimburse those advances by June 30, 2027. Customer Cost Protections A central element of the agreements is the allocation of infrastructure costs. Black Hills says the structure is designed so Google bears all costs associated with serving the planned data center throughout the life of the project rather than shifting those costs to existing utility customers. The agreements include cost pass-through mechanisms, full recovery of generation investment over the contract term, protections against stranded assets, early-termination provisions and collateral and financial-assurance requirements supporting Google’s long-term commitments. House passes ratepayer protection bill to limit data center cost shifts

The bill would “largely reinforce” a transition that is already underway as more states adopt large-load tariffs and is unlikely to pass the Senate before the midterm elections, analysts say.

A Meta data center in Kansas City, Mo. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill on Sept. 16, 2026, that aims to insulate ratepayers from data center-related grid and generation costs.

Courtesy of Meta

This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback .

Dive Brief:

The U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday passed the Ratepayer Protection Act — a bill designed to prevent data centers and other large computational loads from shifting their grid and power generation costs onto existing customers — in a 417-3 vote.

The bill requires states to “consider” adopting a set of standards for loads larger than 100 MW — something that is already underway in most states. T he House bill is “somewhat behind the regulatory curve” and would “largely reinforce” that transition, ClearView Energy Partners said in a client note Thursday.

The bill is unlikely to pass the Senate before midterm elections in November, but could eventually become law, ClearView said. Because of the Senate’s compressed pre-election schedule, passing the bill may require unanimous consent, leaving an opening for senators seeking stronger consumer protections to block the legislation, the research firm added.

Dive Insight:

Although the bill is unlikely to pass soon and would likely have limited impact given the proliferation of large-load tariffs among states, its passage reflects a broad, bipartisan backlash against data center development and AI.

At the same time, utility companies see the potential for significant growth from building the grid infrastructure needed to serve data centers, which can use as much power as small cities. Some have argued that large loads can bring down prices by spreading out fixed costs while spurring grid investment.

State regulators are increasingly looking to codify ratepayer protections through new rules such as requiring prospective large-load customers to pay upfront for system impact studies, ramp up to full load within a set number of months and pay an exit fee if they stop development or significantly reduce service. Only 13 states lack any utility tariffs setting requirements for data centers and other large loads, and at least three of those states were considering proposed requirements as of July, according to a large load tariff database maintained by the Smart Electric Power Alliance.

The Ratepayer Protection Act would require state utility regulators and unregulated utilities to consider adopting large load standards ensuring cost recovery for the “full, incremental” cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade needed to serve the large-load customer.

It would also require large loads to provide financial assurances before grid upgrades are made and guaranteed cost recovery if a large load exits its power supply contract early.

The bill “ensures large data centers pay for the infrastructure they require while giving states the flexibility to determine what works best for their communities,” Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., the bill’s co-sponsor, said in a press release . Rep. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., was the bill’s other primary co-sponsor.

The bill gives state utility regulators and unregulated utilities a year after its passage to begin considering whether they need to adopt large load tariffs or service requirements. They would have a total of two years to make a final decision.

The bill’s inclusion of power supply costs could be significant, ClearView said, noting that interconnection agreements typically only cover transmission and distribution infrastructure.

“In addition to the significant incremental development costs, requiring data centers to [Bring Your Own New Capacity] could extend the construction process of data centers by years, as it typically takes far longer to construct a power plant than develop a data center,” the research firm said.

The bill’s outlook in the Senate is unclear.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. and ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced last month the GRID Savings Act , which is also aimed at protecting ratepayers from data center costs. The bill would require FERC to set rules on large load interconnections, including for cost allocation, financial security requirements and cost estimate disclosure.

Heinrich has said the House bill doesn’t go far enough, according to Politico .

The Center for Data Innovation contends the bill should apply to all large loads, not just data centers.

“Congress should apply the standard uniformly to any customer at 100 MW or more, establishing a separate rate class for these large electricity users,” Michelle Lopes Maldonado, the group’s associate director of AI policy, said in a statement. “This preserves the cost-recovery principle while eliminating sectoral favoritism and ensuring residential users are not left paying the bill.”

LG Energy Solution’s New BESS Qualification Opens Door to AI Data Centre Market

LG Energy Solution’s battery energy storage system (BESS) has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready, giving the battery maker an entry point into the power infrastructure ecosystem being developed around artificial intelligence (AI) data centres. The qualification is significant because AI infrastructure is creating new requirements for power systems, with data centres needing large amounts of electricity while also managing rapidly changing loads and maintaining high levels of power reliability. LG Energy Solution said its BESS meets the applicable requirements for AC energy storage solutions under NVIDIA’s DSX Ready programme. Reference Desing Qualifications  NVIDIA DSX Ready is a qualification programme for partner products and solutions that meet applicable requirements of NVIDIA’s DSX reference designs. The broader NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software as part of the design and operation of AI infrastructure. For LG Energy Solution, the qualification allows its BESS to be positioned as a component within this wider AI infrastructure architecture. The company said its solution is designed to address power-management requirements including AI load smoothing, voltage ride-through and power reliability, while helping customers bring additional power capacity online faster. The qualified system uses modular 2.5 MW/5.1 MWh battery blocks, allowing customers to scale deployments according to their power and energy requirements. Multiple battery blocks can be combined as power requirements increase, giving the system a modular approach to deployment. BESS Incorporation  The BESS also incorporates an integrated AC architecture supporting grid-forming capability, fast response times and voltage ride-through, according to LG Energy Solution. The qualification comes as power availability and reliability become increasingly important considerations for AI infrastructure. Unlike conventional data-centre loads, AI computing workloads can create significant changes in electricity demand, making fast-response power-management systems an important part of the supporting infrastructure. In this context, BESS can act as a power buffer between the grid and the data centre, responding rapidly to changes in load and supporting voltage and power stability. The LG Energy Solution system is therefore being positioned not only as conventional energy storage but also as part of the power architecture required for AI facilities. The company is also expanding its manufacturing footprint in North America. LG Energy Solution said it plans to secure more than 50 GWh of LFP battery-cell production capacity by the end of 2026 through its network of five regional production facilities. Localised Supply Chain The company said its localised supply chain covers battery-cell manufacturing, pack production and system integration. Its ESS portfolio also includes system integration, DC battery containers and PCS-integrated AC battery-container solutions. LG Energy Solution is targeting demand from data centres, infrastructure developments and utility-scale energy storage projects in North America. The company also offers IRA-compliant solutions eligible for applicable Investment Tax Credit incentives, alongside a local service network. “Being selected as a partner for NVIDIA’s first-ever DSX Ready program validates the strength and competitiveness of our BESS products,” said Chang Beom Kang, Head of ESS Battery Division at LG Energy Solution. “Building on our differentiated local manufacturing capabilities and technology leadership, we will further expand our digital infrastructure business and accelerate growth in this rapidly evolving market,” he added. CoreWeave Moves Up the AI Stack

CoreWeave is moving higher in the AI software stack with the launch of CoreWeave Forge, a development environment designed to connect model training, inference, observability, evaluation and post-training into a continuous improvement loop. Introduced at the company’s Fully Connected conference in San Francisco, Forge brings together technologies from Weights & Biases, OpenPipe and the open-source marimo project with CoreWeave’s inference and AI infrastructure services. CoreWeave says the environment remains open across models, frameworks and clouds, allowing production data and agent traces to feed directly into subsequent evaluation, fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning workflows. Canva and MasterClass are among the customers already building with Forge. The platform includes CoreWeave ARIA, now generally available, for analyzing experiments and proposing subsequent runs; Weights & Biases Models for experiment tracking; CoreWeave Notebooks; CoreWeave Registry for versioning models and agent configurations; CoreWeave Sandboxes for isolated agent, reinforcement-learning and evaluation workloads; and CoreWeave Post-Training services spanning supervised fine-tuning, model distillation and serverless reinforcement learning. CoreWeave Inference is also being incorporated into Forge, including a preview capability called RL Rollouts that can hot-load model checkpoints into a live inference deployment rather than requiring the deployment to be recreated during an iterative training cycle. CoreWeave is pairing Forge with a new CoreWeave Partner Network spanning infrastructure, data services, independent software vendors, security, models and inference. The company says participating integrations are validated under production workloads on CoreWeave rather than simply listed in a software marketplace. Initial and existing ecosystem participants include NVIDIA, VAST Data, ClickHouse, CrowdStrike and others, while Exa, Parallel Web Systems and You.com are being integrated as search providers for AI agents. Taken together, Forge and the Partner Network extend CoreWeave’s strategy beyond supplying accelerated compute: the company is assembling a development and operating layer intended to connect the infrastructure underneath AI workloads with the telemetry, evaluation and post-training processes used to improve models and agents after deployment. best_artifact.title: CoreWeave Secures $2.6B Loan as Lenders Take on GPU Renewal Risk
best_artifact.text:
CoreWeave Secures $2.6B Loan as Lenders Take on GPU Renewal Risk

CoreWeave has closed a $2.6 billion delayed draw term loan facility that introduces a significant change to its AI infrastructure financing model: the debt extends beyond the average duration of the customer contracts supporting it. The new DDTL 5.5 facility has an approximate five-year maturity, while the underlying customer contracts average roughly three years, allowing CoreWeave to finance GPU infrastructure tied to shorter-term enterprise commitments rather than requiring contracts that extend through the life of the debt. The structure effectively asks lenders to underwrite part of the residual value and re-leasing risk associated with the GPU infrastructure. When an initial customer contract expires, CoreWeave can renew the agreement or re-lease the capacity to another customer, subject to criteria established in the credit agreement. CoreWeave says shorter-duration contracts can command higher prices and are more compatible with procurement practices among global enterprises, potentially broadening its addressable customer base beyond AI labs and hyperscale customers that can make very long-term capacity commitments. The facility was meaningfully oversubscribed and priced at SOFR + 5.50%, with Ba2 and BB+ ratings from Moody’s and Fitch, respectively. JPMorgan and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group served as joint lead arrangers and bookrunners. Proceeds will fund the purchase and deployment of HPC infrastructure dedicated to customer contracts. The transaction follows CoreWeave’s $3.1 billion DDTL 5.0 facility completed earlier this year and brings the company’s reported debt and equity capital secured year-to-date to more than $30 billion. Key Points • $2.6 billion DDTL 5.5 delayed draw term loan facility • Approximate debt maturity: five years • Average underlying customer contract duration: approximately three years • Financing therefore extends beyond the initial contracted revenue period • CoreWeave can renew contracts or re-lease GPU capacity after the original agreements expire, subject to credit-agreement criteria • CoreWeave says shorter contracts can attract more enterprise customers and often carry higher pricing • Facility priced at SOFR + 5.50% • Moody’s rating: Ba2 • Fitch rating: BB+ • JPMorgan and MUFG served as joint lead arrangers and bookrunners • CoreWeave says it has secured more than $30 billion of debt and equity capital year-to-date 🌐 Analysis The important development is not simply another $2.6 billion entering the AI infrastructure market. It is the transfer of some contract-renewal risk from CoreWeave toward its lenders. CoreWeave’s earlier GPU-backed financing model closely matched infrastructure debt with contracted customer demand. DDTL 5.5 changes that relationship. With roughly five-year debt funding assets associated with customer contracts averaging approximately three years, lenders must place value on the GPUs and CoreWeave’s ability to keep those systems economically productive after the initial contract expires. That is particularly relevant as AI infrastructure moves toward a broader enterprise customer base. Enterprises may be reluctant to make five- or six-year GPU capacity commitments while accelerator architectures, model economics and inference requirements are changing rapidly. CoreWeave can now use infrastructure financing against shorter customer commitments while funding the underlying assets over a longer period. There is a cost associated with that flexibility. That 100-basis-point difference is noteworthy, although the two facilities are not directly comparable solely on spread because their collateral and contractual structures differ. CoreWeave Expands with 360 MW Buildout in Indonesia

Three new facilities scheduled for 2028 will mark CoreWeave’s first data center presence in the Asia-Pacific region. CoreWeave announced plans to expand its AI cloud platform into Indonesia, marking the company’s first data center presence in the Asia-Pacific region. The expansion will add three facilities with a combined 360 megawatts of contracted IT power, with the sites expected to come online in 2028. CoreWeave will own and operate the compute environment across all three facilities and plans to deliver its full AI cloud platform to AI labs, startups, enterprises and public-sector customers deploying workloads across Southeast Asia. The company said the expansion is intended to address growing regional demand for locally available AI infrastructure, particularly for latency-sensitive applications and workloads affected by data-locality requirements. “CoreWeave goes where we can bring AI pioneers the capacity, performance, and reliability they need to build and scale their ideas,” said Sachin Jain, chief operating officer of CoreWeave. “Indonesia is investing heavily in AI education and digital capacity, and it’s paying off—the country is becoming one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing destinations for global tech investment.” The company said the investment supports Indonesia’s efforts to strengthen domestic digital infrastructure and expand local AI capabilities. CoreWeave also plans to recruit and train an operating team in Indonesia, adding a workforce-development component to the infrastructure buildout. The Indonesia project extends CoreWeave’s geographic footprint beyond its current U.S. and European markets. As of March 31, 2026, the company operated 49 data centers globally, with more than 1 GW of active power and more than 3.5 GW of contracted power supporting AI workloads. CoreWeave also cited recent third-party performance benchmarks as evidence of its platform positioning, including MLPerf training and inference results, Platinum rankings in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 1.0 and 2.0, and independent inference benchmarking for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.6 conducted by Artificial Analysis. • CoreWeave is entering the Asia-Pacific region through three new AI data center facilities in Indonesia. • The facilities will provide 360 MW of contracted IT power and are expected to come online in 2028. • CoreWeave will own and operate the compute environments and deliver its full AI cloud platform across the sites. • The expansion targets regional demand for low-latency, data-local AI infrastructure. • CoreWeave plans to recruit and train an operating team in Indonesia. 🌐 Analysis CoreWeave’s entry into Indonesia is significant because it extends the company’s infrastructure strategy into a region where AI demand is rising alongside stricter requirements for local data processing and lower-latency access. The 360 MW commitment is substantial for a first regional deployment and indicates that the company is planning for large-scale AI capacity rather than a limited market-entry footprint. The announcement also highlights a broader shift in AI infrastructure deployment. AI cloud providers are increasingly expanding beyond established U.S. and European hubs to place compute closer to users, enterprises and public-sector customers. For Southeast Asia, this creates additional competition around power availability, data center development, network connectivity and technical workforce capacity. With the facilities not expected online until 2028, execution will depend on construction, power delivery, equipment availability and customer demand. Even so, the contracted capacity gives CoreWeave a defined platform for entering the Asia-Pacific market while extending its existing global buildout. The acquisition moves Vertiv further upstream in the data center power chain as access to utility capacity becomes a constraint on new AI infrastructure. UIG designs power architectures that can combine utility connections, onsite generation and energy storage, including grid-connected, bridge-to-grid and islanded configurations. Its proprietary controls platform and pre-engineered microgrid switchgear coordinate multiple power sources with the data center’s critical power train. Vertiv said UIG’s generation-agnostic approach allows operators to select technologies according to what can be permitted, fueled and financed at individual sites. Founded in 2020 and headquartered in Raleigh, North Carolina, UIG has operations in the United States and Europe and has worked on microgrid systems for AI data center operators. Vertiv said the acquisition would allow it to engage earlier in data center development, potentially defining the power architecture before downstream equipment is selected. The company expects UIG to extend its portfolio from the grid interconnect through onsite power, critical power distribution and cooling to rack-level infrastructure. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. Vertiv expects the acquisition to be accretive to adjusted EPS during the first year following completion. Schneider Brings Software-Defined Control to Voltage Power

Schneider Electric is extending software-defined architecture into the medium-voltage electrical layer of AI data centers, introducing a standardized switchgear platform in which protection, control, monitoring and configuration functions are increasingly separated from customized physical hardware. The architecture is already operating in a live colocation pilot with Equinix, with additional pilots planned through 2027 and broader commercial availability targeted for 2028. Announced at YOTTA 2026 in Las Vegas, Schneider Electric’s Software-Defined Medium Voltage architecture is intended to replace much of the engineered-to-order model traditionally used for medium-voltage switchgear with standardized hardware that can be configured and upgraded through software. Schneider says the architecture can reduce ordering and manufacturing lead time by up to 3× and commissioning and onsite acceptance testing time by up to 2× compared with conventional engineered-to-order MV switchgear. Those figures are based on a comparison documented in Schneider Electric White Paper 303 rather than results reported from the Equinix deployment. In Schneider’s 20-panel comparison, the software-defined configuration required 87% less control wiring, 91% fewer terminals and 85% less copper in the control wiring. The architecture replaces multiple dedicated hardware devices — including protection relays, power meters, transducers, gateways, PLCs and control modules — with standardized hardware and virtualized functions. Protection and control logic, monitoring, diagnostics, cybersecurity capabilities, operational workflows, configuration management and upgrades can consequently be delivered or modified through software. Software-Defined Medium Voltage — Key Points Architecture Standardized MV hardware with protection, control, monitoring and configuration functions increasingly implemented in software Deployment claim Up to 3× faster ordering/manufacturing and up to 2× faster commissioning and acceptance testing Wiring 20-panel comparison: 87% less control wiring , 91% fewer terminals and 85% less control-wiring copper Live deployment Equinix colocation data center pilot Pilot schedule Pilot programs continue through 2027 Availability Broader availability targeted for 2028 The Equinix deployment gives the announcement more weight than a conventional product introduction because the architecture has progressed into live colocation operation. Schneider has not disclosed the Equinix facility, electrical capacity, number of switchgear panels, operating voltage or duration of the current deployment. Nor has it published operational measurements from the pilot demonstrating the 3× and 2× improvements. Schneider instead says pilot programs will continue through 2027. That makes the current deployment an important validation stage rather than general commercial availability. The architectural change is particularly relevant as AI campuses require larger blocks of electrical capacity. Instead of engineering many protection, metering and control functions into site-specific hardware configurations, Schneider is proposing a configured-to-order model built around repeatable hardware platforms. Software can then provide differentiation between deployments and allow functionality to change over the equipment lifecycle. Schneider says over-the-air updates can add features or optimizations without physical hardware changes or operational downtime. Schneider also introduced RM AirSeT 38 Software Defined, extending its SF₆-free AirSeT gas-insulated switchgear portfolio from 24 kV to 38 kV. The system uses pressurized pure air for insulation and vacuum interruption rather than SF₆, fluorinated gases or proprietary gas mixtures. Schneider is positioning the 38 kV platform for hyperscale and colocation environments moving toward 36/38 kV medium-voltage distribution as campus power requirements increase. LiquidStack Launches CDU 2.X for NVIDIA Vera Rubin Era Cooling

Trane Technologies is expanding its LiquidStack direct-to-chip cooling portfolio with CDU 2.X, a new architecture-agnostic coolant distribution unit designed to accommodate changing GPU platforms and rising AI rack densities without requiring operators to redesign the surrounding cooling infrastructure. Introduced at Yotta 2026, the platform delivers coolant flow of up to 3,750 liters per minute at 3.5 bar and is designed to support current AI hardware as well as next-generation platforms including NVIDIA Vera Rubin. The engineering emphasis is on configurability rather than tying the CDU to a single rack or accelerator architecture. LiquidStack supports end-of-row and rack-adjacent deployments, along with configurable control valves, power feeds and redundancy options. Dual-feed A/B power and automatic transfer switch options allow the CDU to be matched to different facility resiliency designs. LiquidStack is also using an ultra-low-harmonics variable-frequency-drive architecture intended to address harmonic distortion at the source, reducing the requirement for additional power-quality components. The thermal design supports facility inlet temperatures up to 45°C and lower approach temperatures, positioning CDU 2.X for the warmer-water cooling architectures emerging alongside higher-density AI systems. The product complements LiquidStack’s larger GigaModular platform, now expanded to 14 MW of capacity. LiquidStack became part of Trane Technologies in March 2026, giving the CDU portfolio access to a broader data center thermal-management organization spanning liquid cooling, facility cooling and heat rejection. CDU 2.X is available for pre-order now, with initial shipments scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027. GigaModular tackles aggregate multi-megawatt cooling capacity, while CDU 2.X focuses on maintaining flexibility closer to the IT deployment as accelerator architectures, flow requirements, rack densities and facility designs change. That distinction becomes more important with Vera Rubin-class systems because cooling is increasingly part of the rack and data-hall architecture rather than a utility that can be specified independently after the compute platform has been selected. The 45°C facility-water capability is also significant. NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin ecosystem is driving greater attention toward warm-water liquid cooling, which can expand the operating envelope for economization and potentially reduce dependence on mechanical chilling where site conditions permit. LiquidStack is therefore positioning CDU 2.X around both the immediate thermal load and the longer infrastructure lifecycle: data center cooling equipment may remain installed across multiple GPU generations even as the compute hardware changes much more rapidly. LiquidStack also enters this product cycle with a substantially different corporate structure than it had when GigaModular was introduced in 2025. Eaton to Acquire COL Group for €810M, Expanding European Power Capacity

Eaton has agreed to acquire Italy-based COL Group from Oaktree Capital Management’s Power Opportunities strategy for an enterprise value of €810 million, expanding Eaton’s European manufacturing footprint and its portfolio of medium-voltage electrical distribution technologies. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. COL Group develops equipment and systems for medium- and high-voltage electrical infrastructure, including medium-voltage switchgear, substation and grid automation, battery control systems and other smart-grid technologies. The company operates facilities in Turin, Milan, Bergamo and Catania. The transaction announcement cites approximately 400 employees and projected 2027 sales of €250 million. For Eaton, the strategic significance extends beyond adding another electrical-equipment business. Eaton says the transaction will expand its power-distribution and manufacturing capacity in Europe at a time of increasing demand from both data centers and utilities. That positions COL’s medium-voltage capabilities upstream in the data-center power chain, where large AI campuses increasingly require substantial utility interconnections, substations, switchgear and power-distribution infrastructure before electricity reaches rack-level conversion systems. Eaton + COL Group: Transaction Overview Transaction Eaton to acquire COL Group from Oaktree Capital Management Enterprise Value €810 million COL 2027 Sales €250 million forecast Core Technology Medium-voltage switchgear, grid automation and modular power systems Italian Footprint Turin • Milan • Bergamo • Catania Expected Closing Q1 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals 🌐 Analysis The COL transaction strengthens Eaton at the medium-voltage layer of the power-delivery chain rather than simply adding rack-level data-center equipment. As AI campuses grow toward hundreds of megawatts and gigawatts, the infrastructure between the utility grid and the IT load—including substations, medium-voltage switchgear, protection, automation and power conversion—is becoming increasingly important to deployment schedules. COL brings Eaton additional European manufacturing capacity in precisely these categories. The acquisition also complements Eaton’s work on next-generation data-center electrical architectures. Eaton has developed an 800 VDC reference architecture as part of its grid-to-chip strategy and is participating in industry work addressing higher-voltage data-center power distribution and safety. The broader portfolio spans switchgear, busway, conversion, protection, UPS, energy storage and thermal infrastructure supporting higher-density AI systems. The transaction fits Eaton’s ongoing concentration on Electrical and Aerospace businesses aligned with electrification, digitalization and AI-driven data-center buildout. Eaton reported $27.4 billion in 2025 revenue and has continued to invest in data-center physical infrastructure, including its acquisition of Boyd Thermal for liquid-cooling capabilities.
